📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Loot boxes, dark patterns, virtual currencies, subscription services, pay-to-win systems, and many other trappings of diabolical digital serfdom all face extensive regulation under the European Commission's proposed Digital Fairness Act, which has been formally presented to EU member states today.
  • You can now read the draft text here on the EU Commission's official site.
  • It has been revealed that here's a summary from me, based on a quick delve through the text.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Loot boxes, dark patterns, virtual currencies, subscription services, pay-to-win systems, and many other trappings of diabolical digital serfdom all face extensive regulation under the European Commission's proposed Digital Fairness Act, which has been formally presented to EU member states today. The full draft text of the regulation leaked earlier in the week. If it passes into law - and there's plenty of debate and revision ahead - it'll have major consequences for the developers and publishers of games like Overwatch, Dota 2, and GTA Online.

You can now read the draft text here on the EU Commission's official site. The organisers have also published an introductory explainer that takes us through the timeline of the Act's gestation, dating back to 2020, and summarises its provisions. If passed, the Act will apply to any tech giant doing business in the EU, not just those based in member states, with individual governments able to impose fines and consumers able to seek financial compensation if they think they've been harmed.

It has been revealed that here's a summary from me, based on a quick delve through the text. The Act proposes a number of provisions regarding "unfair" commercial practices, including omission and distortion in advertising and PR communication at large. Amongst other things, it takes aim at "dark patterns" – that is, "visual, auditory and other components" of online interfaces that are designed to manipulate or deceive. The text also forbids personalised advertising and pricing aimed at children, and prohibits influencers from making "direct exhortations to minors to buy products or to persuade their parents or other adults to buy products in commercial communications".

The items that are probably of greatest interest to us smelly gamers are the passages on virtual currencies, "variable reward systems", and addictive design.

In a recent development, the Act would require game publishers who sell virtual currencies to indicate the real-world monetary value of the currency and anything bought with it. It would also require companies to disable paid-for virtual currencies by default for kids, unless a parent or guardian has given approval.

It has been revealed that as for paid-for "variable reward systems", aka "loot boxes", "surprise mechanics", "Schrödinger's Giftbombs" or however publishers may prefer to describe them, the Act would require companies to state the "types" of object they might cough up, together with the probability of obtaining them. It would also oblige publishers to disable paid-for "variable reward systems" for minors, and give everybody an "easily accessible" way to switch them off.

Sources indicate that the draft Act outright prohibits "pay-to-progress and pay-to-win mechanisms" for kids. More generally, it suggests further constraints for publishers and developers who "design, organise or operate their digital products in a manner that is intended, or can reasonably be foreseen to encourage compulsive or excessive use". Again, it wants companies to give people options to switch these features off.

In a recent development, that includes "features enabling automatic play of content and uninterrupted content consumption without effective and regular interruption moments that enable deliberation by the consumer on their willingness to consume more content". Also, "notifications not triggered by, or not directly related to, the consumer’s interaction or activity on the service", "features incentivising engagement at regular times or with greater frequency, including through penalties or loss of benefits", and "features and system behaviours that encourage continued use by simulating interpersonal relations," such as nagging prompts.

If you'd like a more 'expert' account of the Digital Fairness Act - how dare you! I have read several Wikipedia pages - the bespectacled nabobs of GamesIndustry.biz went and got notes from an actual lawyer. All this follows a change in EU rating law last month aimed at safeguarding the weans from predatory habit-forming devices and instruments of financialisation - games with lootboxes are now PEGI 16 by default, while blockchain games are always rated 18. Across the pond, meanwhile, lawsuits are underway in Fresh York and Washington against Valve's tolerance of lootboxes on Steam, which the lawyers in question define as illegal gambling.

It has been revealed that rockstar has confirmed GTA 6 will officially be playable from midnight on 19th November in your local time zone. If you have preloaded the game, it'll unlock at midnight, and then you can begin playing immediately.

As such, the game will unlock and be available first in Newly introduced Zealand. Availability will then roll out worldwide as each time zone reaches midnight on 19th November.

GTA 6 will unlock and be playable in Newly introduced Zealand first, as it's located in one of the furthest along timezones. The chances are New Zealand is further along in the day compared to wherever you live in the world, so yes, New Zealand will be the first to gain access to GTA 6.

According to recent reports, because of this, there's been a rising trend in people creating New Zealand PSN account to play games as soon as possible. This can be done with GTA 6 too, but you'll need to set up a fresh New Zealand PSN account and buy the game through its PS Store.

Sources indicate that when you have done, you'll be able to play GTA 6 a few hours ahead of other countries like the USA. Keep in mind, though, that you can't transfer your save data from the Upcoming Zealand account you set up to your normal profile.

If you were to play GTA 6 early via the Fresh Zealand method detailed above, you get access to the game at these times:North America: 3am PST / 4am MST / 5am CST / 6am ESTUK/Ire: 11am GMTEurope: 12pm CET / 1pm EETAsia/Oceania: 8pm JST / 7pm AWST / 10pm AEDT.

According to recent reports, GTA 6 is available digitally on the PS Store, or in a basic physical version that ships without a disc. The latter provides a code in the box that you redeem on the PS Store to get the digital version.

The two PS5 digital versions on offer are: Standard Edition and Ultimate Edition.

Ultimate Edition / Ultimate Edition Upgrade Contents:.

It has been revealed that rockstar is only selling GTA 6 in a digital format; you can't buy the game on a physical disc in any way. Even the version you buy in retail shops or from online retailers won't contain a disc. Instead, the actual GTA 6 box will have a code inside you can use to download the game. There's no version with a physical disc of any kind.

Instead, a physical GTA 6 map will be put on the official Rockstar store for $0.99. Or, it'll be included for free in all other purchases from the storefront.

  • According to recent reports, he keeps going: from his other pocket, your wallet.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that you are at, I don't know, some sort of family dining experience. There is a stage. On the stage, there is a magician. You are called up, and made to select a card from a deck of 52. "Don't show me, don't show me", exclaims the sorcerer. There is a dramatic pause, and then he reveals—from his own pocket—your card. Polite applause.

According to recent reports, he keeps going: from his other pocket, your wallet. From his shirt, your wedding ring. Under his hat, your pet hamster, clutching in its teeth a love letter you wrote to your wife when you were first dating. The magician removes his mask—he is you, and you are your wife. Also, throughout this process, someone has given you a backpack and keeps adding exotic hammers to it.

This is what playing Queen's Domain feels like.

According to recent reports, developed, somehow, by a team of two developers, Queen's Domain is a game of constant discoveries. From the moment you wash ashore on the Isle of Neasied, the game just keeps unfurling. It is like some monstrous origami—you unfold one part only to find within it 10 more seemingly impossible sub-folds. Within those? You know it, baby: sub-sub-folds. We are through the looking glass here.

All of Queen's Domain's levels are riddled with crevices, crannies, nooks, and hideaways. Going through them is an experience in seeing some distant ledge, suspiciously flat bit of wall, or oddly aligned geometry and asking yourself "Could I…?" You can. You almost always can, and the game's levels reward your ingenuity and curiosity with upcoming weapons, stat buffs, and strange encounters with stranger NPCs.

According to recent reports, sometimes you unlock whole new regions. Sometimes this is not good. Requiescat in pace to all those who fell down a well and found themselves stranded forever in a beautiful but deadly zone they were approximately 40 levels too underpowered for.

It is the best Dark Souls 1 since Dark Souls 1: unforgiving but almost never unfair, except when being unfair would be funny, and forever dazzling you with masterstrokes of interwoven level design. 16 hours in and hacking my way through a major dungeon, I pulled a lever only to open a door that spat me out right at the game's starting area. I suspect a cross-section of this game's goliath, entwined map would make for a killer bit of wall art.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

It has been revealed that also, you kill like a billion things. Neasied and its sub-environs are filled with freaky creatures—including a fun screeching loot goblin—and it's up to you to put an end to them, which you do via the mechanism of your heaving sack of wunderwaffen. Here is where I warn you, reader: you might be a bit put off by the way Queen's Domain's combat functions at first.

It starts out stiff, stubborn, and idiosyncratic. Even basic enemies take a while to kill and you don't yet have all the tools to deal with them, mobility included. Meanwhile, mechanics like damage being commensurate with your stamina and every single enemy having a rock-paper-scissors-esque relationship to the game's damage types (they're weak to one, neutral to another, and resistant to a third) gives you a whole lot to think about as you try to figure out how to position yourself and swap between weapons without getting murdered.

Stick with it. It's the Morrowind thing: you need that first half hour (and it really is barely more than that) of struggle to appreciate the way your power scales as you unlock newly introduced weapons, acquire more abilities, and—most key—your understanding of the game deepens.

And if that doesn't tempt you, how about this: you like Pokémon? Because it's Pokémon, except your Pokémon are spears and clubs and mauls. You level every weapon independently from your own character level, and when they get high enough, a lot of them literally evolve, like Squirtle, into something upcoming and weird.

At one point in my playthrough, I got stuck in an area for like three hours (I missed something obvious), and didn't even mind; it gave me time to level all three of the game's starting weapons into their bizarre, magical final forms.

In a recent development, I tell you, nothing has smitten me in 2026 like this. It is undoubtedly my personal game of the year, and it might be the first time I've felt that magic I first felt 13 years ago, ensconced in a first-year university flat, playing Dark Souls: Prepare to Die Edition on my PC for the first time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that could a remade Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time be exciting enough to revitalise Switch 2 hardware sales? That was the big question. And early sales figures suggest the answer is yes, it can.

The Switch 2, which had been declining in hardware sales over the last few months, just had its highest (dollar) sales week of 2026 in the US so far following the game's release, according to Circana analyst Mat Piscatella on Bluesky.

It has been revealed that the accompanying Legend of Zelda: 40th Anniversary Edition console in particular is responsible for a notable jump in Switch 2 hardware dollar sales. The themed, special edition console has been popular, with various retailers immediately running out of stock and a rise in scalping.

According to recent reports, it's worth noting that The Legend of Zelda: 40th Anniversary Edition console, priced $520 / £430, does not include a copy of the game. Also, because the console was released 29th October, and the Ocarina of Time remake on 5th November, their sales results will come in separate monthly reports.

The Ocarina of Time launch also caused US hardware spending to jump by 81 percent during the week ending 31st October compared to the same period last year.

Christian Donlan awarded The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time a glitzy five stars in Eurogamer's review, writing: "This is Ocarina as it's always been, as timeless and intricate, but it also has a vibrancy and clarity that makes it feel like it was just created last Wednesday.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Harry Potter film series may have ended in 2011, but its lead, Daniel Radcliffe, remains a household name. He’s made a splash not only by taking on so many “weird” film projects, but he's also made a mark in TV and on Broadway. If you can believe it, the British actor himself noted people told him he would have career troubles after his Wizarding World days. However, Radcliffe ultimately succeeded, and he recently recalled how all that happened..

In a recent development, after Daniel Radcliffe nailed his adorable, precious Harry Potter audition when he was 11, his life would change forever. However, the David Copperfield actor opened on The Old Man and the Three about how challenging it was for him in transitioning to life post-Potter. And I didn’t expect such a brutally honest take:.

According to recent reports, the thing I always say about Potter and what it did for me in terms of like — towards the end of the films I started getting all of us started getting the question a lot from journalists of like, ‘What are you going to do after this?’.... The implication was always like, ‘Well, you're fucked now aren't you? What are you going to do after this? There's nothing left.’ And you know, actually as I look back and I'm like, I can't believe people were saying that kind of stuff to a teenager. It's a really crazy thing to say to a young person.

It's a real shame that people suggested that to Radcliffe and put so much pressure on him at a young age. From the outside looking in, it almost seemed like he was being set up to fail. I can understand that there are many actors out there who are forever remembered for one role. However, that didn't necessarily mean the December Boys actor would be one of them. Radcliffe continued to explain on the podcast that he didn’t let anyone’s negativity bother him:.

So I think there's a thing that happens when part of growing up famous is that as you are trying to figure out who you are, you are getting this perceived version of yourself reflected back at you from like a million places and a million people all the time. And so you have to figure out what of that is not real and what you actually are and what you actually want.

After Radcliffe spent so many years playing The Boy Who Lived, I can really understand why he'd go down a path of self-discovery. Even his Harry Potter co-star, Alan Rickman, advised him and other alumni to try theater. And lo and behold, Radcliffe would eventually star in the Broadway show Merrily We Roll Along, which made tons of money and landed him his first Tony Award.

Plus, we can’t forget that Radcliffe got into “deeply fucking weird” stuff in film projects that would come after Potter. To name a few examples, he played a farting corpse in Swiss Army Man, sported pistols for hands in Guns Akimbo, and showed his dark side while growing horns from his head in, well, Horns. Plus, we can’t forget when he put the weird in Weird: The Al Yankovic, which he described as his favorite film he did post-Potter.

Sources indicate that it goes without saying that Daniel Radcliffe has been quite fortunate, and he can openly admit he hasn't done it alone. He also credits the creatives he's worked with for hiring him:.

So a lot of people were asking us like, ‘What are you going to do after this, and are you going to be typecast?’ And I think there has — I'm sure there is an element of there are some directors out there who particularly in the first few years after Potter didn't want me in their movie because they're like, ‘Everyone will just be seeing Harry Potter when they look at him.’ But for every one of those directors, there was also a director that went, ‘Oh, I would like him in my movie because I want to be the person that reinvents him or that can show an audience this actor that they think they know in a different light.’.

Well, there you go. It appears that directors wanted the credit to be able to help show Radcliffe’s versatility outside of playing a wizard. Of course, many filmmakers naturally become impressed when an actor knows how to step outside of his comfort zone and take on different roles. To that point, Radcliffe’s former Harry Potter director, Chris Columbus, was definitely impressed with the talented actor’s career moves when the franchise ended, saying his projects showed how “fearless” he was.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

Even though Radcliffe received a lot of negativity that his career would end once Harry Potter did, I’m so happy they were proven wrong. And, with that, the public at large has been able to enjoy watching the actor take on a plethora of roles. While the fantasy franchise will always be a career-defining moment, I’m glad that Radcliffe is thriving and continuing to test himself as an actor.

It has been revealed that fans can still revisit the films that first brought fame to the English actor, though as the Harry Potter movies are streaming now with an HBO Max subscription. And don’t forget that the book-adapted TV series will head arrive on that same streamer as part of the streaming schedule on Christmas Day.

Just your average South Floridian cinephile who believes the pen is mightier than the sword.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that black Forest Games, developers of the Destroy All Humans! remakes, have spun out of Embracer Group-owned publishers THQ Nordic via a management buyout and declared plans to form a newly introduced "developer-driven group" of independent studios. The new group, dubbed Third Signal, will aim to "give teams the independence, resources and creative freedom" to "bring their own ideas to life".

Black Forest, based in Germany, announced the move in a press release. "We are grateful to THQ Nordic and Embracer for nine good years and the games we made together," co-boss Adrian Goersch remarked. "Now, we're excited to shape our own future as owners again, to work on an exciting upcoming project with a great team and strong partners behind us.".

Industry observers note that "Some of the best games of the last decade came from teams of fifty, not five hundred," added Third Signal founder Andreas Tobler. "Black Forest Games is one of them, and the right studio to launch Third Signal. Our vision is to build a developer driven group and give teams the independence, resources and creative freedom to continue their creative legacy and bring their own ideas to life." As of writing, Third Signal's website is just a logo splash which promises something coming soon. To be fair, it does also look to have an email address, plus legal and privacy notices. Black Forest's management team will become a co-owner of the studio group as part of this move, but "continue to collaborate on game development tasks" with THQ Nordic.

Recent findings suggest that black Forest had been in the embrace since 2017, releasing both 2020's Destroy All Humans! remake and Destroy All Humans! 2: Reprobed in that time, plus DLC Clone Carnage. Over the years they've also made multiple entries in the Giana Sisters platformer series, survival game Fade to Silence, and 2017's Bubsy: The Woolies Strike Back.

It has been revealed that that's a right old mix of stuff, but the biggest names in it are all resurrections of series or characters created by other folks back in the day. Pandemic Studios in the case of Destroy All Humans!, Accolade in the case of Bubsy, and Germany manufacturer Time Warp in the case of Giana Sisters. That makes the fact it sounds like this move'll give Black Forest a bit more creative freedom intriguing. Here's hoping that if they do blueprint to try and get some more of their own original ideas off the ground, rather than trucking on with a steady diet of remakes and revivals, they manage to stick the landing. It's all fine declaring that a 50 person team can make a top game these days, but that certainly doesn't mean it's in any way easy to pull off.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Australian developer House House has revealed it used generative AI "sparingly" to help make celebrated, indie, multiplayer puzzle game Substantial Walk.
  • In a statement sent to Aftermath - following a judging fallout related to the Independent Games Festival - House House revealed it had used large language models primarily to help debug the game's code.
  • "In the final stretch of Big Walk's development, LLMs were used sparingly by House House to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs," the developer stated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Australian developer House House has revealed it used generative AI "sparingly" to help make celebrated, indie, multiplayer puzzle game Substantial Walk.

In a statement sent to Aftermath - following a judging fallout related to the Independent Games Festival - House House revealed it had used large language models primarily to help debug the game's code.

"In the final stretch of Big Walk's development, LLMs were used sparingly by House House to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs," the developer stated. "In some cases, snippets from LLM responses were copied as a starting point to be modified into game code - we'd estimate that well under 0.1 percent of Big Walk's code had anything to do with this usage, and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game.".

House House added: "The primary use case for House House's use of LLMs was to research, via chatbots, challenges we encountered with third-party code.".

The studio's revelation comes after a sizeable number of IGF jurors - 19 of them - issued a statement saying they would not vote for any game that used generative AI during its development. This was done after seeing "a significant increase" in entry submissions involving generative AI use, which "set off some fairly intense discussion and disagreement across the judge and jury pools". And rather than not vote for these in silence, a collection of jurors decided to take a public stand.

Sources indicate that house House hadn't disclosed Big Walk generative AI use anywhere before disclosing it for its IGF submission. "We have not made any disclosure on Steam as the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage," the studio explained. "We are posting this disclosure as it has become a matter of public interest.".

In a recent development, house House added: "This is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal. We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalisation of this technology, or its treatment as 'inevitable'. We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to video games and our world, and apologise that Big Walk's LLM usage may not meet their standards.

"Significant Walk was developed without an internal AI usage policy in place, and we consider that lack of policy a failure. We will work to have a more comprehensive policy going forwards.".

It's a revelation that's likely to leave a taint of some degree on one of this year's brightest stars - a game Eurogamer awarded a full five stars to in its Massive Walk review.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, fan translations have absolutely exploded in the past few years, but with the rise of generative AI in this sort of project, it's gotten downright exhausting trying to keep track of which ones are actually worth your time. But there are still devs putting in old-fashioned elbow grease to make sure even the most obscure of Japan-only curiosities is made playable by a wider audience. Such is the case with Meremanoid, a PS1 JRPG that's now playable in English for the first time.

Recent findings suggest that meremanoid, originally released in 1999, is a turn-based RPG not entirely dissimilar to something like Final Fantasy VII, albeit at what was surely a dramatically lower budget. Based on an anime that had finished airing a year earlier, it's set entirely underwater, with a world full of mermaids.

According to recent reports, is it good? Well, look – once you start digging deep enough into the PS1 library, you stop asking that kind of question. Instead, the real question is 'Is it interesting?' and it's certainly got enough unique flavor to have entranced the team of hackers and translators who have created the new English patch.

Industry observers note that the wait is over... "Meremanoid" is here! I'm elated to announce the release of our English patch, an amazing work by our team @cargodin.bsky.social, @mistydes.bsky.social, @popipopess.bsky.social, @shentok.com, and mr.nobody. No AI used! Get it at rhpz.org/t/4714 #FanTranslation #Retrogaming.

"To me personally, these obscure games are fascinating, and the PS1 library is a veritable treasure trove of them," Chapu, who hacked the game, indicates in a Reddit post. "I feel anything were there's a language barrier merits a translation. You can probably play, say, a racing or fighting game in Japanese and still enjoy it without understanding the text, but if there's a story involved, that's when I give it a shot!".

It has been revealed that the patch is available via Romhack Plaza, and here's arguably the most important bit: "From translation to graphics to coding, this fan translation project proudly features zero use of AI," the devs say in a social media announcement. Seeing devs take on the challenge of translating this kind of obscurity by hand for sheer love of the game still does my heart good.

They might be a little better known than Meremanoid, but our list of the best JRPGs you can play today has all the essentials.

#16917. There were 47 graphics chip makers in 1998. Where did they all go?

Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rockpapershotgun ↗ Open Full Page

There were 47 graphics chip makers in 1998. Where did they all go?

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1912 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some may find this hard to believe, given the absolute state of the market today, but if you were building a gaming PC in 1998, the hard part wasn’t finding somewhere that had 3D cards in stock for a reasonable price.
  • It has been revealed that in 1998, 47 companies were designing or selling PC graphics, driving a market that hit 130 million units and outsold PCs themselves.
  • According to recent reports, but the Nvidia of the late 1990s and early 2000s was a far cry from the vast (if tarnished) juggernaut it is today, and at the time it wasn’t even the obvious survivor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some may find this hard to believe, given the absolute state of the market today, but if you were building a gaming PC in 1998, the hard part wasn’t finding somewhere that had 3D cards in stock for a reasonable price. It was choosing the right one among a glut of potential, reasonably affordable options.

It has been revealed that in 1998, 47 companies were designing or selling PC graphics, driving a market that hit 130 million units and outsold PCs themselves. Just two years later, at the turn of the new millennium, only 15 remained, and not long after that, there were merely two: Nvidia and ATI, nowadays part of AMD.

According to recent reports, but the Nvidia of the late 1990s and early 2000s was a far cry from the vast (if tarnished) juggernaut it is today, and at the time it wasn’t even the obvious survivor. Research firm 4th Wave put ATI top for 1998 with 24.5 million 3D chips sold, followed by S3 with 15.2 million and Intel, in its first year in the market, with 6.5 million. Nvidia came fourth on 6.4 million. 3dfx, the manufacturer whose Voodoo cards had made 3D gaming on PC a thing in the first place, sold 5.2 million.

In a recent development, each of those companies went under or sold up for one reason or another, but what’s striking is how most did so within a few years of one another. In the four years between 1998 and 2002, the graphics business essentially stopped rewarding whoever had the fastest chip, instead favouring the companies that could iterate the fastest. A new chip every six months or so for the same APIs everyone used, backed by enough capital to ride out the dot-com crash. Nvidia was built for that; almost nobody else was.

The first companies to go didn’t need any help from Nvidia, though. 3D acceleration had made the humble graphics chip a much bigger and more expensive thing to design, and plenty of incumbents that had found their footing on 2D couldn’t afford to keep going. Tseng Labs stopped developing graphics chips at the end of 1997 with roughly $28 million still in the bank, selling its graphics engineers to ATI for about $3 million. Rendition, maker of the Vérité V1000 3D accelerator, agreed to sell itself to memory maker Micron in June 1998, and ATI bought Chromatic Research for $67 million that October.

In a recent development, in its prospectus for its January 1999 IPO, Nvidia warned that PC makers brought out new systems as often as twice a year, on a spring and fall schedule, and that missing one was a serious risk. The firm subsequently reorganised itself around that schedule, releasing the GeForce 256 in October 1999 and the GeForce 3 in February 2001. By 2002, Nvidia’s annual report disclosed that separate design teams were working on several generations of chips at once.

By this point, though, the writing had been on the wall for quite some time. S3, then the world’s second-largest graphics chip maker, wrote in its annual report for 1999 that a graphics chip stayed on sale for 12 to 18 months, and that a delay "as short as a few months" could cost it a design win with a PC maker. Any company that was rolling out just one major chip per year was launching against a rival’s refresh at best. At worst, it was launching late against next-gen chips.

That’s essentially what happened to 3dfx when Rampage, the chip that was meant to succeed the Voodoo5, never shipped. The firm lost its other big advantage around the same time with Glide, its own programming interface that only ran on Voodoo cards. Glide flourished while Direct3D, Microsoft’s rival interface built into Windows, was still lacking features, meaning that plenty of games ran best on 3dfx hardware, but that lead was swiftly eroded once Direct3D and rivals’ OpenGL drivers caught up; developers could now write a game once and run it on anyone’s card. By 1999, Creative was selling Nvidia-based Riva TNT cards with drivers that let Glide games run on them. 3dfx sued, then open-sourced Glide altogether that December.

In a recent development, by then, though, 3dfx had already made its most damaging mistake. A year earlier, on December 14, 1998, it agreed to buy graphics card maker STB Systems for about $141 million in stock, and CEO Greg Ballard said the Voodoo3 would only be sold on 3dfx’s cards. That revelation left Diamond and Creative in a tough spot, having built their gaming lines on Voodoo chips. They were now stuck high and dry without access to the upcoming one.

3dfx was solely concerned with its margins here. The price of its single-chip Voodoo Banshee card dropped from $150 to $89 within a month of launch. With prices in freefall, selling the finished Voodoo Banshee meant that 3dfx pocketed the margin that’d otherwise go to a partner like Diamond or Creative. Those boardmakers inevitably walked, and went where the chips were. STB had been selling Nvidia cards right up to the deal, and its last annual report includes a $3 million note it held from "Nvidia Corporation, a supplier." Creative already had Riva TNT cards on shelves, and Nvidia, which then didn’t make its own cards, would sell its chips to anyone.

Sources indicate that intel, meanwhile, was causing problems from the other end of the market. Its i740 "Auburn" graphics chip launched in early 1998, and Microprocessor Report, the newsletter for the industry’s engineers, argued that Intel’s arrival encouraged Cirrus Logic, Oak and others to fold that year. Just over a year later, after lacklustre sales, Intel confirmed that it was ending support for the i740, then pulled out of standalone desktop graphics chips altogether to put graphics into its motherboard chipsets instead, starting with the i810. This was extremely problematic for companies like S3, Trident, and SiS. They survived on cheap chips for big PC makers, and by the second half of 2001, estimates say Intel’s integrated graphics business had risen to control 55% of the market. That, in turn, pushed S3 to sell its graphics business to a VIA joint venture for $323 million.

Industry observers note that then the money ran out. Venture funding for graphics startups had already dried up in 1999 as the dot-com bubble deflated, and exits inevitably followed. 3dfx lost $100.5 million in the second quarter of 2000, with its CEO blaming a late Voodoo5, and on December 15 that year it sold its assets to Nvidia for $70 million in cash (and a million Nvidia shares) after failing to secure credit. STMicroelectronics, which made the PowerVR-based Kyro II, quit PC graphics in early 2002.

In a recent development, ATI, however, survived alongside Nvidia because it was already operating in the way the fresh market wanted it to. It was the biggest seller at the time, and it made its own graphics cards, which Microprocessor Report said brought in most of its revenue and margin. So, making its own cards wasn’t 3dfx’s mistake; it was locking out boardmakers who had been selling Voodoo cards for it. That pushed those boardmakers towards Nvidia, and a late Voodoo5 and cash crunch dealt the death blow. ATI also used its stock to buy the engineers that its rivals were shedding: Tseng’s, Chromatic’s, then, in February 2000, ArtX’s for $400 million, a team that’d just designed the Flipper graphics chip for Nintendo’s GameCube.

According to recent reports, for the next two decades, the the graphics industry was dominated by ATI - which eventually folded into AMD in 2006 - and Nvidia. For a while, it was a real fight. AMD paid $5.4 billion for ATI, and in the second quarter of 2010, Radeon cards briefly overtook Nvidia in discrete graphics shipments. However, AMD had a problem: it couldn’t really afford ATI. It wrote off $1.6 billion of goodwill from the deal about a year after it closed, and its PC chip business kept struggling.

Recent findings suggest that by early 2015, AMD’s CPU and GPU revenue was down 38% on the year, and the organization was close to negative book value. Its quarterly R&D budget had fallen to its lowest level since 2004, with Nvidia spending nearly half as much again. Radeon cards stayed on the same Graphics Core Next architecture for about seven years before RDNA arrived in 2019. By then, Nvidia had already rolled out its RTX cards with dedicated ray tracing hardware and Tensor cores for AI, and it never gave that lead back.

Industry observers note that intel was the only company with pockets deep enough to try breaking back in. Its first go, Larrabee, was cancelled as a consumer graphics chip in December 2009. It finally got there in 2022, when the Arc A770 went on sale from $329, alongside the cheaper A750. Both arrived after repeated delays and struggled with older DirectX 9 games, and many observers - RPS included - put their chances of breaking up the Nvidia-AMD duopoly at low. By the time then-hardware editor James returned to the A750 in 2023, Intel had drastically improved its drivers, bringing big gains to both general performance and DX9 compatibility. Even then, the Arc series had yet to prove it could work well at launch, without the need to be ironed out across months of updates.

The second generation did indeed fare better, with the Arc B580 successfully selling out at $249 in December 2024. But that still barely impacted the wider industry, with Intel sitting at just 1% of graphics card shipments in the third quarter of 2025 and around 2% this spring, when Nvidia took roughly 90% of the 12.5 million cards shipped.

It now looks like Intel is on its way back out of gaming graphics cards. In April, leaker Jaykihn claimed that its next-generation Celestial gaming cards had been cancelled "long ago," and the latest rumours say B580 supply could be cut so Intel can sell more Arc Pro cards for, surprise surprise, AI work. It’s important to note that Intel hasn’t confirmed any of that, and one of its execs has said that Arc isn’t leaving its PC roadmap. Still, Intel had everything 3dfx didn’t: the cash, the PC makers on side, and the same APIs as everyone else. But money can’t buy two decades of Nvidia and AMD fixing their drivers game by game, and it seems to have decided its capital is better spent on AI anyway.

Evidently, the question of where all the other GPU makers went does not have one single answer. Some couldn’t afford the rising costs, some couldn’t keep pace with a newly introduced Nvidia chip every six months, and some lost their cheap business to Intel’s integrated graphics or went under when the dot-com bubble burst. Left over was a Nvidia/ATI (later AMD) duopoly, and PC gamers haven’t exactly done well out of it. We saw the RTX 4080 launch at $1,199 in 2022, nearly twice the 3080’s price, and the ongoing, AI-driven RAM shortage has pushed prices higher still.

In 1998, 47 companies wanted your money. Now there are two, and the bigger one, Nvidia, sells nine of every 10 graphics cards - yet still makes most of its money from data centres. Eighteen years on, it's a bad time to be a PC gamer, and nobody’s in a hurry to make things any better.

For those who don't know, this is a fancy android handheld console, a sort of beefed up DS for the modern handheld aficionado.

Recent findings suggest that "Arguably too many layers of abstraction," writes Douse. Arguably too many layers of abstraction pic.twitter.com/VjW0IX00Gg.

As highlighted by CEO of esports tech giant 100 Thieves Alex Wechsler on Twitter, the game looks to be ported pretty well to the phone, with mobile touchscreen controls viewable on both sides of the screen. Be warned though, as confirmed by Wechsler in a Twitter reply, it'll get your phone running hot.

As a father of 2 kids and always having wanted to play WOW, I’ve finally found a way 🥹 pic.twitter.com/eIVn0gn1WC.

This coming alongside World of Warcraft: Forever's built-in (and very good) controller support could mean the game has real potential to spread far and wide across the vast array of different hardware out there. Blizzard has already hinted at plans of porting the game to other platforms, so who knows? Maybe we can expect an official mobile port to tread the path paved by these community-made mods.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Slay the Spire 2 has a new character—notably, a new character in testing—and as the patch notes themselves point out, that testing will very much be needed: "We expect to make a great number of content and balance changes before the Fool is ready for the main branch.".

Industry observers note that I decided to hop into the beta branch myself and take her for a whirl, and—yeah, those changes'll have to come. The Fool's central mechanic is her bow and arrow—she can fire an arrow/shoot card to deal damage equal to the card's base damage plus her aim. So if a shoot card deals 15 damage and she has six aim stocked, she'll deal 21.

Industry observers note that this is a little busted, because by default, the Fool has 6 aim already put in her bank. Her non-strike starter card, Foolish Shot, already deals a hefty 15 damage for just one energy. With aim, the first time she uses it, it deals a whopping 21 damage, which is a heck of a damage output for the Fool's first round of combat.

The saving grace here is that when a card that fires an arrow is used, that arrow becomes lodged in a target, who gains the Impale status. You can't play any more arrow-based cards until you either Dislodge (another game term, hence the proper nounage) an arrow with a card that dislodges, or until you have more than one arrow.

Industry observers note that in my runs, I wasn't able to figure out the latter. But I really didn't need to, because I was one-shotting bosses the whole way up the spire. One card in particular, Repeat Shot, seems borderline broken. While it is a rare, it shoots a target for 20 damage (when upgraded) X times, plus your current aim.

With precious little setup, I was casually knocking (or should I say nocking) out around 78 damage on turn one just by having the card pop into my hand. Add even a little aim generation to your deck, and Repeat Shot solves single-target fights for you. By making them dead.

There are some other interesting mechanics, too, such as a trio of melodies you can activate and trigger other cards off of. Wah Blast, for instance, hits twice if you've got a Cho or Ki melody active. There's also Stretch, which gives you extra block on the usage of your next block card, Sadness, a status card that can be turned into Joy which gives you energy and card draw, and tarot cards via a power called Mythic Form.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Obviously, she's broken. I absolutely shouldn't be one-card tapping bosses on Act 1 just because I happened to first-turn draw into a single rare card. But she is already very fun, and I look forward to seeing what more balanced version of The Fool will look like in the full game.

Industry observers note that other than that, the testing branch now has two new modes: Blitz, a more bite-sized version where there's no map or gold, and Dread, which appears to be an Ascension+ mode for masochists. Could never be me.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arc Raiders, Embark Studios' popular extraction shooter, has exceeded 17m copies sold, according to publisher Nexon.

Sources indicate that arc Raiders was released at the end of October 2025, so reaching that milestone in a year is nothing to scoff at. According to Nexon's latest earnings report, however, only 1m copies of those 17 were sold in the third quarter - meaning sales have certainly slowed down.

Relatedly, Nexon mentioned it expects Arc Raiders' revenue to decline in the fourth quarter compared to the same period last year - when the game enjoyed its hugely successful launch - and anticipates revenue will be "broadly flat sequentially". Despite this, the company said Arc Raiders' revenue was "within the outlook", naming its Frozen Trail update as a key moment that brought back some lapsed players while introducing upcoming ones.

Indeed, Frozen Trail boosted the game's Steam player count, and reports suggest it also helped Arc Raiders hit a six-month player high across various platforms.

Even with its slowing sales, Arc Raiders remains one of Nexon's most successful titles. The tech giant primarily attributed an overall year-on-year revenue increase, for the nine months ended 30th September, to the game.

Looking ahead, the biggest question hanging over Arc Raiders is whether or not it's going to get a dedicated PvE playlist. Following a successful test earlier this summer, Embark has been coy, and hasn't stated whether PvE will return as a permanent feature. Arc Raiders' Chinese version does have a dedicated PvE mode, and executive producer Aleksander Grøndal said he could see both PvP and PvE modes co-existing in the future.

For example, the magazine kicks off with a statement from Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, who discusses the past 25 years of the brand and where it's going in the future - similar to a statement she shared on social media recently.

This time though, she talks less about how games will be made, and more about the fact that she wants to take "creative risks" while also acknowledging that her team won't "get every decision right" along the way.

Here are the key parts of the statement:.

Sources indicate that "There are plenty of milestones from the past 25 years, and you'll find many of them in these pages. But I don't think the story of Xbox is really a story about any given hardware, launch or number. It is a story about people. Players turned games into friendships, rivalries and family traditions. They played with roommates who became lifelong friends, with brothers and sisters who moved across the country, with parents who got older and kids who eventually picked up the controller themselves. Some of the people we played with 25 years ago are no longer here. Some are sitting next to us, now playing with a upcoming generation.".

In a recent development, "We should be proud of that history. But we shouldn't be trapped by it.".

Industry observers note that "Games are alive. The best ones find latest players and new creators. They move between generations. They get changed, remade and occasionally broken apart and rebuilt into something nobody expected. Twenty-five years in, Xbox should have that same restlessness.".

"We have been given the chance to care for some of the most loved games and characters in the world. Our job is to protect what makes them special without protecting them from change. To keep making new things. To take creative risks. To meet players wherever they choose to play. And to make sure someone discovering Xbox for the first time today can feel the same possibility that someone felt turning on that first console in 2001.".

"We don't get every decision right. No organization that is still making things does. But we can keep listening, learning and building. Twenty-five years ago, a relatively small group of people imagined that Microsoft could make a game console. It was an improbable idea. They made it real. I like that as our inheritance.".

Sources indicate that there's definitely some interesting stuff in here, including Sharma's insistence that Xbox shouldn't be "trapped" by its past, that her team should be willing to experiment and take risks in the future, and an admission that not every decision will work out for the best. That's pretty refreshing to hear, and it certainly reads well on paper at least.

Industry observers note that let's see what happens, eh? Xbox's 25th anniversary has been a weird year, full of ups and downs, but it seems like there's a cautious optimism circulating around the fanbase regarding things like console updates, exclusives and various other initiatives that have been introduced since the Xbox CEO took the helm at the start of the year.

These next 25 years are going to be fascinating to say the least!

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake only just released on November 5, but it's already become the best-selling physical release of the year in the US, a record that'll surely hold against another highly anticipated game releasing in a few days that rhymes with Grand Theft Gelato.

It has been revealed that per Circana's Mat Piscatella, citing sales data through November 7, Zelda: Ocarina of Time is the first physical launch to surpass 1 million units sold in the US since Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom from 2023, further cementing the new remake as an undeniable commercial success, in case there was any doubt. And yet, with GTA 6 looming on the horizon, Ocarina of Time's days as the year's best-selling physical release are likely numbered.

Now, you could make the valid argument that GTA 6 technically isn't getting a physical version considering it's a code-in-box situation where you receive a physical game case but have to download the actual file by typing in a code. In essence, a digital game code inside of a physical case for collectors. That noted, Piscatella confirmed in a follow-up post on Bluesky that Circana counts a code in a box as a physical sale, so GTA 6 will definitely qualify at least according to Circana's methods.

After just one week in market, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is 2026's best-selling physical video game in the US. It is the 1st title to surpass 1M physical units in a US launch week since 2023's The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom. Source: Circana Retail Tracking Service.

According to recent reports, it's not a huge surprise to see the Ocarina of Time remake selling so many physical cartridges considering its strong nostalgia appeal, not to mention excellent reviews calling this one of the best remakes of this generation. Our own 5/5-star review calls it  "a remake for the ages, blending the charm and whimsy of the original with more digestible gameplay and stunning visuals.".

As GamesRadar+'s Anna Koselke writes, "It's as timeless as it ever was, managing to recreate one of the most beautiful games to date without compromising the magic of its 1998 predecessor – only adding to it. Between newly voiced dialogue, revamped dungeons, fresh puzzles, and more, Hyrule has never felt so alive.".

Zelda: Ocarina of Time is a masterclass in remakes, Final Fantasy Resonance lead states on the back of reviving one of Square Enix's dead mobile JRPGs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that back in July, Doom developers id Software laid off around a hundred people as part of wider Microsoft blood-letting. Now, a few of those devs have founded a fresh employee-owned studio, Hidden Horses. Their first project is Danger Pay, a single-player FPS influenced by ancient arcade blaster Smash TV (pictured) and dystopian movies such as deadly gameshow fable The Running Man – itself an influence on Smash TV.

Industry observers note that hidden Horses have 20 id Software alumni on the books, including former lead VFX artist Todd Boyce, principal engine programmer Dustin Land, senior AI and gameplay engineer Daniel Young, producer Andrew Willis, senior technical designer Jordan Turner, principal technical designer Tim Locke, and senior skybox artist Allison Dombek. They're looking to make "the kind of old school shooters that we think people want more of," in Land's words.

According to recent reports, all members of Hidden Horses own a share of the company, with bosses "democratically" appointed, in the words of a FAQ. "Our structure is quite flat, and we elect leaders when needed," Willis told Vertical Slice in a separate interview. "Financially, this means we are not subject to investor demands and the preservation of the company and the jobs it sustains is paramount over needless growth and our 'capital' doesn't compete for returns with other potential investments.".

All of which is obviously gesturing towards the horse elephant in the room: Microsoft, who've made enormous cuts to their Xbox biz in their eagerness to further supercharge their $4 trillion market value.

"We've replicated some things, changed some things, and added others [from our id Software days]," Willis went on. "Overall, I think top-down hierarchy is something we all have bad experiences with—we also don't want to trend chase or make a game by focus group. We want to make the kinds of classic gameplay focused games that we would play ourselves. We think there is a market for that and our experiences with the gaming community in our past work history informs that.".

Industry observers note that willis's hope is that the "flat" structure will motivate staff to work harder, because they feel like they have a meaningful say over the company's direction. "It allows all ideas to be considered and means we don't miss out on any contributions from our employees just because they don't sit high up in some arbitrary hierarchy," he said..

According to recent reports, I'm cynical about "flat" organization structures, myself. I think they are very often just an excuse for the biggest egos in a company to throw their weight around. It can work given a friendly initial mix of founders, but it gets complicated when you start hiring new people who don't have the same chemistry. Mind you, there are no plans to expand the company dramatically for the foreseeable. "We want to create a vehicle that allows us to make games for our livelihoods, not to make crazy profits and get 100x returns," Willis went on. I'm also a bit leery of the fact that Hidden Horses have popped up a Kickstarter, because I'm leery about crowd-funding in general, even when Peter Molyneux isn't involved. The studio founders are presently working on some promotional initiatives to drum up support, including a studio documentary and *squints* a promotional beer? Still, I'm happy to hear that at least a few Cacodemon wranglers jettisoned by the big M have landed on their hooves feet. I wish Hidden Horses the best of luck with it all. As for Danger Pay, proper screens, footage and release details are to follow.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that according to Valve, average framerates are derived from players running the game on their Steam Decks, assuming they've opted in to provide framerate data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Valve has released a new Steam patch that adds Steam Deck framerate data to a game's store page, giving potential buyers an indication of how well a game runs on the handheld.

According to recent reports, as per Valve's announcement post, average framerates are now listed in the Steam Deck Compatibility section of a game's store page, but you'll need to click Learn More to see it. Additionally, the feature is only available for games that have been tested for Deck compatibility - those with Verified, Playable, or Unsupported badges - so while it's not a complete list, it still covers thousands of titles.

Industry observers note that according to Valve, average framerates are derived from players running the game on their Steam Decks, assuming they've opted in to provide framerate data. And the store widget also includes another helpful addition: a histogram displaying the percentage of data samples. This demonstrates how often a particular framerate has been reported, and is useful in determining if the game's framerate is sporadic, such as due to stutters.

"The current Steam Deck Verified compatibility rating is based on standardised test criteria, but it may not match every customer's bar for acceptable gameplay," Valve explained of the upcoming feature.

Sources indicate that "This is especially true around performance - a game with an Unsupported rating due to unstable performance may be considered playable by some customers, and a Verified game may not reach a framerate that some customers prefer to play at. By providing average framerate data for each game, customers now have a more complete picture of how the game performs on Steam Deck and can make more informed purchase and play decisions.".

In a recent development, currently, Steam's framerate data feature only covers performance on Steam Deck, and for a very good reason: Valve's handheld has standardised hardware, so the results will be the same for all players. However, Valve says it intends to provide framerate data for more devices in the future, but it's not clear if that's ever going to include desktop PCs, considering the complex nature of their hardware configurations.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Disk Cleanup, our regular weekend feature delving into the PCs of PC gaming luminaries. Come back every weekend to read a new interview, digging into the crucial questions, like "How tidy is your desktop?" and "What game will you never uninstall?".

Stuart Ashen—better known by his YouTube persona Ashens—grew up on a diet of 8-bit games on consoles like the Atari 2600 and the Spectrum. The earliest PC game he recalls playing was Syndicate Wars on his first home-built rig—a Pentium 200 MMX machine housed in a server tower case: "I loved Syndicate. Hated Syndicate Wars. Never got on with it at all," he states. "Ended up giving it to a friend who loved it … I think I went on to Duke Nukem 3D or something.".

Alongside his video work, Ashens is presently making a folk horror film told in reverse. "Unfortunately, it's far enough away from release that there's no point plugging it," he says. But he hit pause on production to guide me through the haunted arcade of his PC. We talked DOS fighting games, the problem with rangers in RPGs, and the worst retro game Ashens has ever played.

I'm currently playing Gloomhaven, the digital version of the board game, for the second time. I put about 150 hours into it, then sort of left it, and I've come back to it.

Sources indicate that it's kind of fantastic. I love board games, but Gloomhaven is one I didn't think I would ever play, because I know it takes two hours to set up or something. When the computer is taking control of all the bits and bobs, you can play it on your own in the background while you're doing other things and waiting for stuff. That’s going to get a lot of time from me.

It's all team-based. It's all your standard band of different [fantasy] archetypes together, and then after they reach a certain level, that's not true. When they do a certain personal quest thing, which can be a pain in the arse for various reasons, they retire, and then you can replace them with other ones you've unlocked. So the team basically changes, and the whole dynamic changes over time, which is something that's really kept me interested.

Recent findings suggest that the previous game would have been Baldur's Gate 3, and it is still installed. I should uninstall it for two reasons. One, it takes up a lot of space, and two, I might start playing it and it will eat all my spare time again. Because, yeah, I got kind of obsessed.

From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews.

Recent findings suggest that to give you an idea, I'm now on 350 hours on Gloomhaven, but 927 on Baldur's Gate. Probably a good 50 to 100 hours of that is just sitting in the background [but] it's so far ahead of any other game I've played in terms of hours, it's unbelievable.

It has been revealed that I've never played a Larian game [before], and I didn't like the early Baldur's Gate games. I got the first one free with a graphics card. I remember opening the graphics card box and about 14 discs fell out. I was so excited to play it and I could not get on with the combat. It was that weird, sort of concern commands and pause and do things. It just didn't do anything for me, and I thought, "Oh, that's disappointing." After a couple of hours, I never came back to it.

And then I saw something about Baldur's Gate 3—because I wasn't interested in it at all for obvious reasons, and it just had that spark to it of, "Hang on, there's something special going on here, with the writing of that." And then I saw they changed the combat to turn based, and I was like, "Right, sign me up.".

I bought it, installed it, started playing it, and that was the only thing I played probably for two and a half, three years.

This isn't one I played a lot—we have this because we were streaming it. But it's Street Fighter for DOS from 1988.

Recent findings suggest that it's entirely different to the arcade version, I think it's got more in common with the weird Commodore 64 version. But basically, we were going through, on stream, every single DOS fighting game, and it's pretty bad. But weirdly, not as bad as a lot of them.

In a recent development, DOS fighting games are, like, for every good one, there's five really bad ones and one that you can't believe they'd charge money for. It barely works. I love fighting games, so it's always interesting to see these obscure ones we haven't heard of. But God, the DOS ones! It was like they saw Mortal Kombat but absolutely did not understand Mortal Kombat. So you've just got teenagers dancing around in front of a camcorder, badly digitised, and some Christ-awful game engine that just does not work fundamentally.

Then again, the arcade game is awful for the first Street Fighter. There's just not really much of a game to it. Even in the arcade, it's all about learning the special moves and repeating them over and over. Or trying to, because the controls are not quite there for Street Fighter 1. I think that's got to be one of the biggest improvements in history, from Street Fighter 1 to Street Fighter 2.

That is Baldur's Gate 3, with 927 hours.

I think I [initially] did a Ranger. I'm always interested in Rangers in RPGs, because they're never implemented very well. In EverQuest, it was the [class] that could dish a lot of damage and yet couldn't take any. It was just noticeably inferior …. It felt better in Baldur's Gate 3. It probably wasn't the optimal build, but it did actually work. I do like the ranged bow combat, and I'm always interested in why they never get it right. Is it just nobody likes Rangers, but they feel they have to put them in anyway?

I didn't go Dark Urge until the second playthrough, not really understanding what it was at the time, obviously. And then I was informed after, "Oh, you should try that." And I'm like, "Oh, this is what the game was written for. OK, yes, it's even better now.".

Sources indicate that it's absolutely incredible. Writing, performance, everything is a step above anything that had come before, I think. And the combat is so much fun, which obviously is super crucial because that's a huge percentage of it.

Industry observers note that that is Command & Conquer 3: Kane's Wrath. Because sometimes, if I've got 10 minutes spare, I'll just quickly start up a skirmish map on it, just a simple 1v1, and see how quickly I can win, and that's it. It's almost a comfort thing. I only do it once maybe every couple of months, but I'll always leave it installed for that reason. Plus, by today's standards, it doesn't take up much room.

Industry observers note that I think I like the skirmish better in 3, due to the variety of all the bits and bobs in it. It's probably not the tightest of the games in the series. But for me, that's the one I always enjoyed the most.

It has been revealed that there's a little window, and you type in the name of any file on your PC, and it's already indexed them, and it instantly appears with where they all are, and you can easily narrow things down. Life changing. The amount of files I've given stupid names to, or put in the wrong folder that I've just found immediately because of this. It's fundamentally changed the way I work.

In a recent development, oh dear. So I have icons turned off on the desktop. I'm going to turn them back on, if I can remember how.

Fuck! I'm turning that off. Oh no, that's not good. That's pretty bad. Oh God! How do I turn them off? Oh God, it's horrible.

Sources indicate that it's just two 4k monitors entirely covered in icons and stuff. Because I don't use the desktop at all, so I just let it auto install things there and forget about it. I've got a little program called RocketDock, which keeps the useful things on the side of one of the monitors, and that's it. I've not looked at the actual desktop in years, and it is monstrous.

One I only briefly played back in the day, and then something made me play it again on stream, and it was so much better than I remembered, [is] Moonstone for the Amiga. It's like a hack 'n' slash-y, brawler type thing, but with a lot of RPG elements. It's also beautifully designed, with really nice artwork and sound. But it's a really interesting game. No other game quite has the vibe of it. Not to say it's the best game ever or anything, but it's still very bloody good.

What is the worst overall? Oh man, there's so many bad ones. There's one called, which we keep talking about [on stream], Graeme Souness Vector Soccer. This isn't the worst. I'm just going to mention it because it's great. It's an Amiga game, and literally the characters are vectors. But of course, due to the way they didn't really have the processing power back then, these vectors look like the Keep Britain Tidy logo. So they're all weird things moving around and the frame rate is monstrous. It's like three frames a second. It's totally unplayable. Nobody seems to know if there's a good game under the hood or not.

Industry observers note that I think for absolute worst, it's got to be SQIJ! And it's for the Spectrum. There are versions for other computers that are perfectly competent. But the Spectrum one was written by a man, or a boy at the time, bless him, called Jason Creighton, who really didn't want to fucking write it or work at that company again. So he just spat out something absolutely awful that basically is borderline unplayable, sent it to them, and they just didn't bother looking at it. They just loaded it, went 'Oh, that loads.' Put it on tape, out it goes.

Powerhouse, the company that released it, released it twice—a standard release and then a release later on as a compilation. As released, it doesn't work. Basically, Jason accidentally turned on the caps lock or something in the source code, and you can't turn it off, and the keys actually don't function if caps lock is on. So you load it up and you can't move. That's it. Fortunately, it's so badly put together you can literally break into the program and turn the caps lock off through poking a memory access directly, if you know what I mean. And by the time you've hacked it to work, it's just no fun whatsoever.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that CD Projekt Red have reportedly enlisted Ukrainian AI firm Respeecher to modify voice lines recorded for the Polish version of Geralt of Rivia in The Witcher 3's upcoming Songs of the Past expansion.
  • According to recent reports, game File report that after suffering a stroke in 2019 and having to rehabilitate his speech, Rozenek was able to record some lines as Geralt for a quest in The Witcher 3's 2022 next-gen revision, but that doing so left the actor "so exhausted".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that CD Projekt Red have reportedly enlisted Ukrainian AI firm Respeecher to modify voice lines recorded for the Polish version of Geralt of Rivia in The Witcher 3's upcoming Songs of the Past expansion. The move's been made with the permission of Geralt's Polish voice actor, Jacek Rozenek, and is rooted in the studio wanting his fresh lines to sound similar to the ones he recorded for the original game prior to having a stroke which has altered how he sounds.

According to recent reports, game File report that after suffering a stroke in 2019 and having to rehabilitate his speech, Rozenek was able to record some lines as Geralt for a quest in The Witcher 3's 2022 next-gen revision, but that doing so left the actor "so exhausted". With next year's Songs of the Past expansion, CD Projekt Red were seemingly more concerned about making sure lines recorded by post-stroke Rozenek don't sound markedly different to those he recorded a decade ago for the base game and its existing expansions.

Recent findings suggest that after a meeting between the two sides confirmed that Rozenek's voice had grown lower and gruffer due to some combination of the stroke and him simply getting older, the studio made the decision not to recast the actor, but instead let modify Respeecher modify his lines to make them sound closer to those original recordings. Rozenek reportedly gave his blessing for this to go ahead. "The point is that this voice should be as close as possible to my voice from 12 years ago," he told Game File. "I have great trust...for the creators of this game.".

Industry observers note that this isn't the first time CD Projekt Red have enlisted Respeecher's services. Back in 2023, it was revealed that the studio had used speech synthesis software to make ripperdoc Viktor Vektor's lines in the Polish version of Cyberpunk 2077's Phantom Liberty expansion sound like actor Miłogost Reczek. Reczek died in 2021 before he could reprise his role as Vektor for the DLC, so rather than recasting the character across the whole game to avoid noticeable differences in voice, CD Projekt got another actor to voice Vektor's new lines for Phantom Liberty, then used the genAI tech to make those lines sound like Reczek was delivering them. CD Projekt Red noted at the time that they'd gotten permission from Reczek's family before going ahead with their strategy.

Speaking to Game File about this latest use of genAI on Rozenek's Songs of the Past lines, CD Projekt localisation producer Mikołaj Szwed noted that "as a person working with voice actors over all the regions in the world, this is a big concern". "I do think this is one of those ways where you can use AI ethically, with consent and also to do something good," he added. The argument the studio are making at current is that this was "a special case" due to Rozenek's specific situation with Songs of the Past.

Geralt's English voice actor Doug Cockle reportedly won't have his lines for the latest expansion get the same genAI treatment, nor will any lines Rozenek records for future Witcher games, with the studio seemingly happy to lean on the passage of in-game time as an explanation for Geralt sounding different in the latter case.

As ever, there's a debate to be had as to whether CD Projekt Red should have simply recast Rozenek's role in Songs of the Past if the difference bothered them so, possibly while bringing the actor on to help tutor whomever his human replacement for Songs of the Past would be in nailing the exact gravelly tone needed for Geralt. That way, you'd have two actors being paid for work rather than forking out for genAI instead of one of them, though it's possibly an idea that'd only work well in theory. If I were Rozenek I'm not sure I'd be totally happy aiding someone who could potentially be tapped to replace me going forwards, though it does very much seem like the lesser of two evils when compared to the potential of voice actors being replaced by genAI line readings.

According to recent reports, as far as the game alone is concerned, I'm also not sure Geralt's voice being different in the new expansion is something that'd bother me too much when playing. One would assume he'd not suddenly be sounding like a member of Alvin and the Chipmunks, and there are plenty of storyline justifications you could concoct or lean on for him sounding that bit gruffer at times.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rockstar Games has today clarified a few remaining details about Grand Theft Auto 6's framerate target and visual settings on PlayStation 5, PS5 Pro and Xbox Series X/S. And as part of the same announcement, the developer revealed a key detail about the game's cloud streaming options.

GTA 6 will be available to stream via Xbox Cloud Gaming. However, this is only possible on Xbox Series X/S consoles, as well as - surprisingly - the last generation console, Xbox One. Notably, that means you can't use Xbox Cloud Gaming to stream to PC, or other devices, despite it being useable there.

According to recent reports, you may recall that in early October, a Verge report stated Microsoft had acquired exclusive cloud streaming rights for GTA 6, with the understanding being that the game would be available to stream on any XCloud-supported device - as in, to PC as well. Xbox immediately shot down the report, saying GTA 6 "will not be streaming exclusively or to PC".

Recent findings suggest that perhaps more surprisingly, the cloud-streamed version will be using Series S graphics settings, not those of the more powerful Series X console. Considering the loss in quality inherent in cloud streaming, this will make for a less-than-ideal way of experiencing the game.

Beyond cloud streaming, GTA 6 supports Remote Play on PlayStation and Xbox, so you can stream the game on your local network to any device, from a PS5 or Xbox Series X/S console.

GTA 6 pre-loading is now available across PlayStation and Xbox. The code-in-box physical editions have also started shipping, letting you claim the code and pre-load your copy in time for GTA 6's 19th November launch.

Sources indicate that ever since the Scrubs revival made its way onto the 2026 TV schedule, I’ve been tuning in, and it really hasn’t disappointed. Last season was good, but I think Season 2 has been especially stellar, and that has a lot to do with what subject matter is getting the spotlight. The fresh season reeled me in with Dr. Cox’s health developments, but now I’m really hooked thanks to what’s going on with J.D. and Elliot’s relationship. And, I think it’s time I discuss it.

In a recent development, when Scrubs returned to TV, I was instantly taken aback by the choice to make J.D. and Elliot exes. Bill Lawrence defended the decision to CinemaBlend months ago, saying that the couple just couldn’t go a few episodes without “being a horrible couple,” so he wanted to be realistic.

While it bummed me out at first, I’m starting to really appreciate the sort of nuanced conversations that come with J.D. and Elliot no longer being together. They’re both still co-workers and co-parents, so they have to make it work as friends, but I just don’t feel like I see enough relationships like this on TV. My own parents have been divorced for awhile, and I’ve watched their relationship evolve in a latest way amidst still being my parents. I know it’s quite common, and yet, for many TV couples it’s either them being together or not.

In a recent development, on that topic, the episode from a couple of weeks ago, “My Story,” really threw me for a loop in the best way. In it, we’re led to believe that J.D. and Elliot end up going to dinner together and deciding to try to make things work again. We learned more about why things fell apart between them, too. But ultimately, we learn the whole scenario is happening in J.D.’s head, and he decides not to pursue their relationship in fear of hurting her once again.

Sources indicate that I’m all for love, and a part of me wants to see these two back together, but I'm also really enjoying seeing this unique dynamic on Scrubs. There’s clearly a lot of real love between them, but they were also famously on-again-off again throughout the original run of Scrubs. It feels like we’re getting to watch these two attempt to heal in real time and decide how to go forward in their lives, between being busy medical professionals and being parents, too.

Industry observers note that I guess for the time being I’m not thinking about whether I want them together ultimately or not, I just want to continue to see this difficult dynamic between them be explored. I think Scrubs is one of those few shows that can simultaneously be hilarious and emotional, and I think what’s going on between J.D. and Elliot is something worth stretching out for a while.

Star Wars Galactic Racer is my favourite game of the year so far. It's an incredible racing title that even surpasses the original Star Wars Episode 1 Racer in my view, and I've had so much fun with the campaign and online multiplayer.

Recent findings suggest that there's just one downside that everyone's been pointing out since it was revealed, and that's the absence of local split-screen multiplayer. With that in mind, the development team have found a way to implement it in a newly introduced revision.

The enhancement isn't available yet, but will be coming to the game in early 2027. Alongside it will be a newly introduced mode called Free Play, which is where you'll be able to freely choose your vehicle, character, planet and race track.

In a recent development, "We’ve heard you! Local split-screen multiplayer racing is coming in early 2027. A dedicated team at Fuse Games has been working hard to bring a brand fresh mode, Free Play, to STAR WARS: Galactic Racer. This new mode will allow you to choose your vehicle, character, planet, and race track to race alone or with up to 3 other players in local split-screen action.".

Recent findings suggest that it seems Free Play is the only place where you'll be able to access local split-screen multiplayer in Star Wars Galactic Racer, but that's no surprise considering how solo-focused the main campaign is. They'd literally have to rewrite massive portions of the campaign if they were going to implement split-screen into it.

Anyway, this is just an amazing bonus on top of an already amazing game, and I encourage you to check it out if you enjoy a title like Burnout 3: Takedown - it's fast-paced and frantic, has the same kind of takedown system that you'll remember from that game, and the roguelite campaign is really well designed (online is great fun as well).
