#16897. Amid soaring PC hardware prices, gaming monitors are getting cheaper and cheaper. Here's why, and what to buy

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2080 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rockpapershotgun ↗ Open Full Page

Amid soaring PC hardware prices, gaming monitors are getting cheaper and cheaper. Here's why, and what to buy

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2080 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hello, good local-time-zone-adjusted afternoon, and let's just say it's been a while.
  • Industry observers note that instead I speak of screens, where there is actually some very good news.
  • Also bear in mind we've had a fair old bit of inflation in recent years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hello, good local-time-zone-adjusted afternoon, and let's just say it's been a while. But I come back to you now at the turn of the technological tide. Well, sort of. Sadly I'm not here to predict an end to the ridiculous AI-fuelled chip crisis. That whole mess has a couple of years to run, surely.

Industry observers note that instead I speak of screens, where there is actually some very good news. In short, have you seen how cheap PC gaming monitors are? I mean remarkably, almost stupendously, cheap. I'm talking £60 / $60 for an entry-level 1080p panel with triple-digit refresh rate, sub-£200 / $250 for high-refresh 4K gaming. Heck, even OLED monitors now start with a "2" in both currencies.

Also bear in mind we've had a fair old bit of inflation in recent years. A 4K panel bought today for £200 is equivalent to paying roughly £150 back in 2020. All the while, that same £200 / $200 right now won't buy you a current-model gaming graphics card at all, even the most feeble example, and will barely secure a basic dual-channel 16GB DDR5 memory kit. Youch.

So, I think we can all agree monitors are cheap in the current chip-catastrophe context. The immediate question is why? The answer isn't all that complicated, actually. Most obviously, the display market isn't being devoured by the AI craze. All those data centres are stuffed with GPUs, memory chips and NAND flash, not monitors.

By way of example, one of the largest new AI data centres on Earth is Microsoft's new Fairwater site in Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin. It's thought to pack hundreds of thousands of Nvidia Blackwell GPUs. The cost doesn't bear thinking about, but those GPUs are built into what's known as "headless" server racks. In other words, they have no screens at all. Ultimately, the key compute hardware is all managed remotely, in which capacity the Fairwater facility is reported to at the moment have around 375 employees. If we generously assume each has two PC monitors, that's only 750 for the entire site.

According to recent reports, AI isn't really driving demand on the end-user side of the equation, either. Put it this way: you don't need to buy a latest phone, laptop or PC to access the latest models. At the same time, the display market is suffering from something of a glut of overcapacity. Chinese companies built out huge capacity in LCD panel manufacturing over the past decade, to the extent factories are now running underutilised. Meanwhile, even the OLED market is arguably oversupplied.

In fact, Samsung and LG, the two big noises in large OLED panel manufacturing (as opposed to OLED displays for tablets and phones), have been shifting emphasis away from TV panels to PC monitors because the latter offer better margins. Meanwhile, the AI boom has almost definitely meant lower demand for new PCs. Certainly, the big research houses point to cratering PC sales thanks to higher component costs. Long story short, that's oodles of capacity combined with weakening demand. Like I said, the explanation for cheap monitors isn't exactly rocket surgery, if you know what I mean.

What is a bit more complicated is making sense of what's available today in the gaming monitor market. With so much choice, where exactly is the very best value to be found? And are there any remaining pain points?

According to recent reports, monitor specifications, to be sure, can be tricksy at the best of times. But if you're looking for some blanket rules to fling casually over the whole LCD monitor market - I'll be digging deeper into OLED tech another day - try these for size. Look for, at minimum, 300 nits brightness and 1ms response times. Refresh rates are a slightly more complicated call, but for the vast majority of games, 144Hz is plenty. For "esports-grade multiplayer fare like Counter-Strike or Dota 2, or I think a refresh in the high 200s will get the job done for most. If you'll benefit from more than that, you almost certainly know who you are already.

Oh, and heavily favour IPS over VA panels. Exceptions exist: there are some decent "Rapid VA" panels these days and Samsung, in particular, does some nippy VA models. But a lot of the cheaper stuff is pretty slow and smeary, making VA a risky buy. Finally, don't worry too much about claimed HDR capability, save for the fact that HDR 400 certification at least means the monitor can do 400 nits. Unless a monitor has local dimming, it won't be truly HDR capable.

Anywho, one immediate and rather ironic issue is the growing mismatch between monitors and GPUs. For sure, it's great you can grab a high-refresh 4K monitor for such little money. It's almost hard to believe that you can have this 27-inch IPS MSI for sub-£200 (you're looking at $250 for the same model in the US), and it even has a 288Hz 1080p dual mode.

I actually favour 32 inches with my 4K gaming, and that's naturally a little pricier, especially if you insist on an IPS - which again, you probably should. But even $350 for that kind of panel (here's a comparable model for £340 in the UK) is a fraction of what you'd have paid for a similarly specced model a few years ago. And it probably wouldn't have included dual-mode functionality.

Here's the problem, though. How are you going to drive the thing, what with its eight million-plus pixels? After all, the cheapest RTX 5090 on Newegg right now is over $6,500. So high-end Nvidia GPUs now cost about as much as a decent used car.

Recent findings suggest that of course, you might be surprised just how effective the likes of an AMD RX 9070 XT or Nvidia RTX 5070-class GPU is at 4K thanks to upscaling technologies including DLSS and FSR. The latest transformer model upscalers really do knock out pretty stellar image quality. Add in a bit of frame gen and you have a compelling combination of visual sharpness, reasonably low latency and nice smoothframe rates, even in the most demanding of games. Perhaps the one thing you can't do is enable full path tracing in a game like Cyberpunk 2077 and still expect a slick experience, but standard ray tracing remains an option.

The bigger snag, unsurprisingly, is that you can no longer bag a 5070 at (let alone below) its original £539 / $549 MSRP. Instead, you're looking at the thick end of £800 / $900. That's a bit of an ask for pairing with a £200 monitor, isn't it?

According to recent reports, I'd therefore argue that, for pure gaming purposes, the bang-for-buck sweet spot remains just where it's been sat twiddling its thumbs for the better part of a decade, namely 1440p. That applies to both its vanilla 16:9 aspect variety and my personally preferred ultrawide format, the latter being so very immersive and also pretty nifty for daily multi-tasking. Indeed, the 27-inch 1440p segment even brings the vibrant colours and infinite contrast of OLED panels into a reasonably affordable window.

By way of example, £179 (or $150) is enough for a circa 200Hz, IPS 1440p panel with super low (by IPS standards) pixel response, even if the 250-nit brightness is lower than I'd like. Meanwhile, as I write these words, pricing for big-brand 27-inch 1440p gaming OLEDs kicks off at about £290 in the UK and roughly $270 in the US. Admittedly, those entry-level OLEDs come with some compromises, which I'll cover in a forthcoming post. But what you might call 'proper' OLED panels can be had around the low £300 / $300 mark - not throw-away money, for sure, but relatively accessible.

The 34-inch 1440p ultrawide segment is a bit trickier, however. The good news is that conventional LCD models can be had for relative peanuts, with prices starting at about £220 or $249 for game-focused, high-refresh models. But those two example both use a VA panel, which usually means inferior pixel response.

IPS models are a little thin on the ground when it comes to 34-inch ultrawide, but sneaking in below £300 / $300 is generally possible. The real bummer is OLED, where going ultrawide invokes a massive premium. The best price I can find on a big-brand 34-inch ultrawide today is $629 for this Asus model in the US and £648 for this MSI option in the UK.

In a recent development, that's awfully toppy, especially when you consider that you can grab a 49-inch, 5,120x1,440 ultrawide OLED for barely any more money. I do actually quite like those 49-inch ultrawides, but I have to concede the ergonomics are challenging. However, 4K OLEDs in 27-inch and 32-inch formats can also be had for as much as £100 / $100 less than the current cheapest 34-inch 1440p ultrawides, which doesn't make much sense to me.

Recent findings suggest that again, with 4K, there's the challenge of keeping all those pixels updated. If you already have a sufficiently mighty graphics card, though, I a 32-inch 4K OLED can make a fantastic all-round option, and something like this MSI model for £549 would be absolutely lovely. You get good pixel density and lots of space for daily desktopping, plus OLED visuals and a large enough panel to be really get you into your games.

It's just a pity that 34-inch OLED ultrawides remain so weirdly expensive, it being a format that ticks so many different boxes. As for my own personal money-no-object pick, well, I'm typing these words on the newly introduced Alienware AW3926QW, the 39-inch 5K2K beast with a Tandem WOLED panel and RGB subpixels.

One could argue it's a relative steal at £1,079 or $1,100. I mean, it's pretty much peak current PC gaming display technology, and it's about half the price of what Nvidia's second-tier RTX 5080 graphics card is going for lately. Assuming you can even find one in stock.

At this point, the one major category I haven't covered is LCD monitors with mini-LED full-array local dimming. Cards on the table, I'm not a huge fan of mini-LED monitors. The detailed reasons for that are, perhaps, the subject for another day. But I've reviewed countless models and have yet to see one that didn't come with pretty serious compromises.

It has been revealed that that remarked, the technology has gotten a lot more accessible in the last 12 to 18 months, to the extent that 27-inch 1440p models start at just over $250. I've had that specific model in and came away pretty impressed. It's very, very punchy, and even factoring in the limitations of mini-LED versus OLED when it comes to lighting control and speed, I cannot deny the temptation.

Sources indicate that just for completeness, one further exception to the general rule of cheap gaming monitors involves ultra-high refresh monitors aimed at serious esports aficionados. I'm talking about panels like this 1,000Hz LG I sampled elsewhere. At £800 / $1,000 for a 25-inch 1080p IPS panel it's inevitably a niche proposition, and poor value by normal standards.

I think a much better compromise for just about everyone, short of an actual esports pro, is to grab a larger, higher resolution monitor that offers one of those windowed 1080p modes running at about 500Hz or thereabouts. That way you've got a nice high-res panel for both work and play, as well as that ultra-low latency mode for when you want to dance around Dust 2 doling out the headshots or whatever.

Incidentally, I realise I've gone in a bit hot and heavy with the OLED content here, the implicit assumption being OLED is all that, and notably without addressing the obvious objections like the risk of burn-in. But all that, I hope you'll be pleased to hear, is very much the subject for my next RPS post on all things OLED.

Industry observers note that until then, all I can say is thank goodness PC monitors provide relative respite from the parlous state of much of the rest of the PC component market. It's absolutely brutal out there if you're building a gaming PC, but at least you'll get a lot of screen for your money.

Just to round things out, if anyone has any specific queries at any given price point, form factor or panel type, shout out below and I'll try to steer you in the direction of a decent model.

Europe is about to get very tough on loot boxes in games, according to a leaked draft of the landmark Digital Fairness Act

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (645 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An alleged draft of the potentially game-changing Digital Fairness Act has leaked ahead of its scheduled publication tomorrow (11th November), containing proposals that could dramatically affect the way games operate and are monetised within the European Union.
  • The draft, published by French publication Contexte (via Video Games Industry Memo) goes as far as to recommend that loot boxes (uncertainty-based rewards) be turned off by default for minors, as well as the sale of in-game items and currencies.
  • "The digital era has fundamentally transformed consumer experiences," the draft of the Digital Fairness Act begins.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An alleged draft of the potentially game-changing Digital Fairness Act has leaked ahead of its scheduled publication tomorrow (11th November), containing proposals that could dramatically affect the way games operate and are monetised within the European Union.

The draft, published by French publication Contexte (via Video Games Industry Memo) goes as far as to recommend that loot boxes (uncertainty-based rewards) be turned off by default for minors, as well as the sale of in-game items and currencies. There's also a recommendation that all players - not just minors - should be able to turn off offers related to these lootboxes and gambling mechanics.

"The digital era has fundamentally transformed consumer experiences," the draft of the Digital Fairness Act begins. "It has enabled faster, more convenient and wider access to an ever-increasing range of goods and services. At the same time, it has given rise to upcoming and more sophisticated ways of influencing consumers' choices.

"Along with the indisputable benefits in choice and efficiency, the extensive use of digital technologies allows both old and new unfair commercial practices to affect consumers at scale, exacerbating risks to their economic interests, as well as to their mental and physical wellbeing. Vulnerable consumers are particularly affected.".

Industry observers note that the Digital Fairness Act calls for greater transparency around a "transactional decision". Which means: "Price transparency on the real value of in-app purchases using virtual currencies and the probabilities of winning for virtual offers with uncertainty-based rewards (loot boxes).

"All consumers can turn off virtual offers with uncertainty-based rewards. Some spending-maximising practices prohibited for minors, with the remaining turned off by default. Supporting self-regulation for video games and legal obligation for video games to have an age-appropriate rating. All consumers can turn off attention-maximising features, with some prohibited for minors and the remaining turned off by default.".

"Spending-maximising" refers to systems that pressure us to spend more money than we want to, such as reward systems or pay-to-progress or pay-to-win systems. They're all being targeted here, as is virtual currency, which provides a layer of abstraction as to the real cost of goods.

"It may be difficult for minors to resist such perceived pressure to pay," the Digital Fairness Act said with regard to progression-linked systems. "Therefore, where a product is directed at minors or when the trader is aware with reasonable certainty that the product is used by minors, pay-to-progress or pay-to-win mechanisms [...] should not be made available to minors.".

The Digital Fairness Act is a forthcoming European legislative proposal designed to patch consumer protection rules for various digital dangers that we face today. Importantly, it's not law yet, and it has iterations and discussions to go through before it will be. A timeline on the Digital Fairness Act explainer website suggests it could be adopted late in 2027, then applied more broadly by 2030.

It's also hoping to tackle many things besides shady video game monetisation, including "problematic" influencer marketing, "unfair" pricing practices - such as obscuring the real cost of something until you've progressed through layers trying to buy it - and mysterious-sounding "dark patterns". These relate to 'easy to sign-up, hard-to-cancel' processes, it seems.

These changes aren't happening in a vacuum. Earlier this year, the well-known European age-rating body PEGI announced historic alterations to its game-rating criteria, with an eye to better categorising the dangers of loot box-containing games and aggressively monetised games. These changes have already started to roll out and mean that a game like EA Sports FC, which was previously routinely rated PEGI 3, now automatically gets a PEGI 16 rating because of its Ultimate Team card pack (loot box) system.

The effect of the Digital Fairness Act could tip the balance against these systems being included in games at all. Expect more discussion and digestion of the proposed changes as the Act is officially published tomorrow.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's no secret that the Covid-19 pandemic saw a lot of people using videogames to stave off lockdown blues, and the Jackbox Party Pack games were especially well-suited for the role: easy-to-understand party fare that's optionally family-friendly and easy to play over a video call. PC Gamer mentioned as much back in March 2020.

In a recent interview with PC Gamer associate editor Ted Litchfield, Jackbox Games CEO Mike Bilder said that the pandemic proved transformative for the developer.

"The industry at large obviously saw a lot of success at that time, but we did as well, and we went from a gamer name to a household name," he remarked, noting it was an "unfortunate period of time for the world, but for the gaming industry, a good one, and for Jackbox, a good one as well.".

Industry observers note that "That was kind of a leveling up for Jackbox as a company," stated Bilder. "Suddenly office workers are doing happy hours and families over weekends are connecting over a game of Quiplash or something because it's what you did when you were locked down. People realized how easy it was to just share the screen over a Zoom call and everyone's playing.".

It surprised employees at the studio to see how popular the games had become.

Chief marketing officer Brooke Hofer recalled a scene in the 2022 Knives Out sequel Glass Onion, where characters could be seen playing Quiplash over a Zoom call: "I remember when we all saw that in the studio, and we're like, 'Whoa,' you know. But that was so many people's experience at that time, and it was cool how that was captured in pop culture in various ways.".

As Grand Theft Auto 6 preloads go live, developer Rockstar has detailed the enhancements coming to the PS5 Pro version of the game, confirming these won't include framerates above the 30 FPS its targeting for consoles.

Rockstar shared the news in a blog post released to announce that GTA 6 pre-loading is now available ahead of its release date on 19th November.

It has been revealed that "Grand Theft Auto 6 has been fully developed from the ground up to provide the best possible experience for the current generation of consoles," Rockstar states. It goes on to reconfirm GTA 6 is targeting 30 FPS on all consoles, saying the game is pushing modern machines "to their absolute limits" in order to "bring the vast and rich world of Leonida to life — while maintaining the density and visual fidelity of all its environments and inhabitants.".

Recent findings suggest that PS5 players can expect high-fidelity haptic feedback through the DualSense controllers, improved spatial audio, and Tempest 3D audio, while PS5 Pro enhancements come in the form of PSSR support and ray tracing shadows, which should make the game look especially fancy, plus improved load times. PlayStation players can also expect remote play support. As for the Xbox, the post clarified details on Xbox Cloud Gaming, which will allow the game to be streamed to Xbox consoles including the Xbox One. Notably, this won't work on PC.

Grand Theft Auto 6's 30 FPS target was previously confirmed by Rockstar back in August, but there was some uncertainty around a possible 60fps performance mode at the time. Still, those PS5 technical boons do a lot of work to improve the games it's applied to, which if nothing else should mean GTA 6 will be quite the looker.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

MINTROCKET, Pugstorm, and Fireshine Games have announced a two-way crossover for both DAVE THE DIVER and Core Keeper. Starting November 30, players will be able to unlock the crossover content through a series of missions in DAVE THE DIVER, while Core Keeper players will simply need to update the game. The crossover content is free to owners of each game and will be available permanently once activated.

In DAVE THE DIVER, trouble comes to Otto and Sammy’s farm when Dave plants a mysterious clump of moss from deep underground. Overnight, the moss spreads across the fields, unleashing an invasion of Cavelings from Core Keeper. Armed with a pickaxe, Dave must defend the farm in a upcoming Core Keeper-inspired combat minigame, battling pickaxe-wielding Cavelings and fireball-hurling Caveling Shamans while clearing away the moss to stop more enemies from appearing.

It has been revealed that players who complete the crossover mission can earn special rewards, including the Spicy Lure Charm, which speeds up crab trap catches, and collectible Caveling and Caveling Shaman figurines to display at the sushi bar. The mission becomes available by redeeming a special coupon code after unlocking the farm following Sammy’s VIP event.

Sources indicate that in Core Keeper, Cobra joins the underground adventure as a fresh merchant, bringing a collection of familiar faces and items from the Blue Hole. Players can adopt Momo and Mini Dave as pets, decorate their bases with sushi bar furniture and a custom Blue Hole-inspired scene, and equip Bancho’s signature sushi chef armor. Other additions include a new harpoon gun, green tea, and the Reef Shark as a catchable fish. The crossover also features original DAVE THE DIVER sound effects, including the voices of Dave and Cobra.

According to recent reports, the free crossover update arrives November 30, 2026, with DAVE THE DIVER content launching first on Steam and console platforms to follow. Core Keeper players can access the upcoming content on all platforms from November 30 simply by updating their game. The crossover content will be available perpetually in both games once players activate it.

DAVE THE DIVER is available now for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series, Switch 2, PlayStation 4, Xbox One, Switch, PC via Steam, Epic Games Store, and Microsoft Store, iOS, and Android.

Core Keeper is available now for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series, Switch 2, PlayStation 4, Xbox One, Switch, and PC via Steam.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Considering we're just a few days away from the release of GTA 6 on November 19th, we're bound to start getting reviews at some point between now and launch, and it'll be fascinating to see what the critics think of it!

Recent findings suggest that this is a series that has consistently dominated on Metacritic over the years - a website that takes loads of professional reviews and creates an average score based around them. Grand Theft Auto V has a 97 average rating on there, for example, while GTA 4 goes even higher with a 98 rating.

Recent findings suggest that in fact, every mainline release since GTA 3 (not including stuff like Chinatown Wars and Liberty City Stories) has reached at least a 95 on the platform. To put that into context, the best-rated Xbox Series X game of the year on Metacritic right now is Hades 2, and that game has a 95 average rating.

If we're going off history alone, GTA 6 has every chance of becoming the highest-reviewed game of 2026 on Xbox and PS5. The question is whether it'll manage to hit those highs once again, or whether it'll struggle to meet the hype.

Let's not forget there's never been a wait like this for a GTA game before, and while absence definitely does make the heart grow fonder, it also creates a sense of expectation that's extremely difficult to live up to.

It has been revealed that we'll have to wait and see what happens! You'll find a review roundup on Pure Xbox ASAP, and it seems the smart bet is at least a 95 rating on Metacritic, although that's much easier mentioned than achieved.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen may be best known for their shared role as Michelle Tanner on Full House, but the child actors -- who eventually left Hollywood -- also launched their own cinematic universe of sorts. In the '90s and early 2000s, the duo starred in several TV and direct-to-video movies. For the longest time, most of these movies were only available to fans who owned the hard copies, but that’s starting to change as a handful of their movies have popped up on Prime Video (though one of my favorite titles hasn't been added).

Recent findings suggest that unlike most movies that are released, the highly successful Olsen twins managed to retain all the rights to a majority of their films after buying out the co-founder and former manager of their entertainment firm, making them their own bosses. This allowed Mary-Kate and Ashley to control how their films were distributed and thus kept them off streaming services. It’s unclear what has changed, but it seems like the Olsens have realized how sought-after these films are to their millennial fans and have started to loosen the reins. As a fan of the Mary-Kate and Ashley Cinematic Universe, I’m ecstatic.

As of writing this, eight Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen movies are right now available to stream for Prime Video subscription holders. Four of them are from the early days of the twins’ career and were filmed while Full House was still airing new seasons. The titles include To Grandmother’s House We Go, a Christmas movie and the first of their television films; the Halloween flick Double Double Toil and Trouble; It Takes Two, a loose book-to-screen adaptation of Mark Twain’s The Prince and the Pauper; and How the West Was Fun.

In a recent development, there are also four films from the twins’ post-Full House days, including Passport to Paris, Billboard Dad, Switching Goals and one of my personal favorites and their final movie, Newly introduced York Minute. Needless to say, this is a sweet lineup, but can I just take a moment to highlight one flick that's not present?

While the rest of us were being "normal kids," the Olsen twins were busy producing and starring in a total of fourteen movies between 1992 and 2004. Eight films aren't a bad start, but there are still a lot that need to be added to complete the Mary-Kate and Ashley Cinematic Universe. However, there is one movie that I need to be added ASAP: the 2001 flick Holiday in the Sun.

In the film, Mary-Kate and Ashley play the Stewart twins, whose parents surprise them with a trip to Atlantis Resort in the Bahamas over their winter break. I vividly remember being in awe, listening to “Island in the Sun” play as the twins jet off to the Caribbean. And if Prime Video needs another reason to get the rights to Holiday in the Sun ASAP, it also serves as Megan Fox’s film debut.

Sources indicate that as bummed as I and several other Olsen twin fans are that Holiday in the Sun isn’t one of the eight featured on Prime Video (as of now), it doesn’t put too much of a damper on the reveal. After all, we’ve waited years for even one of their films to hit streaming services, and now we have access to half their filmography.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

Despite there being no official word from Prime Video, news of the release did travel fast on social media, with fans sharing their joy on X:.

In a recent development, I guess it’s time for me to pause my marathon of watching all the upcoming and upcoming Christmas movies and head over to Prime Video to revisit some of these gems. Maybe if enough of us watch, the streamer will add Holiday in the Sun or any of the other Olsen twins movies!
